Cette séance vous permettra de simuler la dynamique proie-prédateur entre du phytoplancton (que l’on notera “P”) et du zooplankton (que l’on notera “Z”). Nous implémenterons des modèles de type Lotka-Volterra avec R sous RStudio. Nous utiliserons plusieurs méthodes d’intégration numérique (= plusieurs manières de résoudre les équations du modèle), soit avec l’intégration d’Euler, soit avec la fonction lsoda, ensuivant ce que nous avions déjà fait lors du premier TP. Cette fois, il n’y aura plus une seule variable (et donc une seule équation à résoudre), mais deux variables en intéraction : les variations de l’une dépendront des valeurs de l’autre, et réciproquement. Il y a aura donc 2 équations à résoudre simultanément. On parle de “système d’équations”.

# 1. Simuler le modèle de Lotka-Volterra

Nous allons ainsi simuler la dynamique d’une population de proie (P) et d’une population de prédateur (Z) suivant le modèle de Lotka-Volterra : - Dynamique de la proie P : dP/dt = + r.P - a.P.Z - Dynamique du prédateur Z : dZ/dt = + e.a.P.Z - m.Z

La proie P a une croissance exponentielle (taux de croissance : r) mais est consommée par un prédateur Z (relation linéaire, taux de prédation : a). Quant au prédateur, il croit grâce à la prédation de manière linéaire (efficacité de la croissance par prédation : e) et a une mortalité linaire (taux de mortalité : m).

## Définition des paramètres et de plusieurs tableaux

<span style="color:red">This code chunk is given directly to us in the TP.</span>

```{r}
# Defining the model parameters
r <- 0.5  # growth rate of the phytoplankton (d-1)
a <- 0.1  # predation rate of the zooplankton feeding on phytoplankton (d-1m3gC-1)
e <- 0.9  # efficiency of the predation (unitless)
m <- 0.5  # mortality rate of zooplankton (d-1)

# Declaring the model time steps

t0 <- 0   #initial time
dt <- 0.01 # time step
tf <- 40  #final time
times <- seq(from=t0, to=tf, by=dt) # time vector
n <- length(times) # size of the time vector: we will use C later

paste("Length of times:", n)

# Declaring the vector for the concentrations of phyto and zoo
mespop <- matrix(0, nrow = 2, ncol = n)

# Declaring the initial values for the phyto and the zoo
mespop[1,1] <- 12  # Initial density of phytoplankton (gC/m3)
mespop[2,1] <- 6   # Initial density of zooplankton (gC/m3)
```

Nous allons maintenant écrire les équations du modèles puis les résoudre, d’abord avec la méthode d’Euler, ensuite grâce à la fonction lsoda.

## Option 1: Intégration numérique selon la méthode d'Euler

Commençons par appliquer la méthode d’Euler, à la main, pour remplir le tableau qui contient les concentrations en phyto et en zoo au fur et à mesure de chaque pas de temps. Pour ça, on utilise une boucle “pour”.

<span style="color:red"> First step: Use the for loop to perform Euler integration. This part is very very similar to what we've done in prior TPs. Specifically in TP1, they walk you through how to construct a for loop and i'm pretty sure give the exact code to use. My approach to coding is usually "find something similar to what i need, copy paste, and edit the details", you could pull that here. </span>

<span style="color:red"> In order to do Euler integration, we need to define the formulas for dP and dZ. These were given to us in class, the "hard work" here is essentially to turn the formula from class into an R equation. We know that $dP/dt = rP - aPZ$ and $dZ/dt = eaPZ -mZ$. From this, we can determine that $P(t) = P(t-1) + dt * dP/dt$ (and the same for $Z(t)$) </span>

```{r}
# "i" here iterates through each column in our matrix mespop. We created mespop with length(times) columns, thus "i" here is a proxy for time.
# And as a reminder the first row of the matrix is phytoplankton, the second is zooplankton
# Note that we're iterating for all values of i between 2 and n (inclusive). We deliberately don't start at 1, that column is already filled with the default starting values !!
for (i in 2:n) {
  # Creating variables to define the previous Phytoplankton and Zooplankton, which will be the column before the "current" column i.
  P_prev <- mespop[1, i-1]
  Z_prev <- mespop[2, i-1]
  # Populating phytoplankton. P(t) = P(t-1) + dt * dP/dt
  mespop[1, i] = P_prev + dt * (P_prev * r - a * P_prev * Z_prev)
  # Populating zooplankton. Z(t) = Z(t-1) + dt * dZ/dt
  mespop[2, i] = Z_prev + dt * (e * a * P_prev * Z_prev - m * Z_prev)
}

# View the final values of mespop
mespop[,n]
```

<span style="color:red"> On to plotting !! We're gonna mimic the plots that were provided by the prof, using base R. The first plot is of Time vs. Populations, thus we know that we need three vectors of data -- a time vector, a phytoplankton vector, and a zooplankton vector. We defined `times` right at the beginning, that'll work great. Our two species vectors are the two rows of the matrix. </span>

<span style="color:red"> As y'all have probs noticed, building plots with base R involves repeated calls that stack on top of each other. I'm gonna start by plotting phytoplankton and then layer zooplankton and the legend on top of that. </span>

```{r}
# X = x-axis = vector of times
# Y = y-axis 1 = phytoplankton = first row of the matrix
plot(x = times, y = mespop[1,], type = "l", col = "green", 
     xlab = "Time (années)", ylab = "Populations (concentrations)", main = "Simulation proie-prédateur")
# Y = y-axis 2 = zooplankton = second row of the matrix
lines(x = times, y = mespop[2,], col = "red")
# Legend
legend("topright", c("Phytoplancton", "Zooplancton"), lty = 1, col=c("green", "red"))
```

<span style="color:red"> For the phase portrait, we note that the x axis is phytoplankton and the y axis is zooplankton. </span>

```{r}
plot(x = mespop[1,], y = mespop[2,], type = "l", col = "black", 
     xlab = "Phyto", ylab = "Zoo", main = "Portrait de phase")
```

## Option 2: Fonction *lsoda*

Vous allez maintenant implémenter le même modèle mais cette fois en utilisant la fonction lsoda du package deSolve (https://desolve.r-forge.r-project.org/). Si ce n’est pas déjà fait, vous devrez installer le package avant de le charger.

Pour simuler ce modèle avec R, il faut fournir à R : 1) les paramètres du modèle (on peut les écrire sous la forme d’un vecteur) 2) les conditions initiales (valeurs des variables au départ) 3) le modèle écrit comme une fonction R (décrivant l’évolution des variables, i.e. leurs dérivées) 4) un algorithme d’intégration numérique (pour intégrer les équations du modèles), ici lsoda 5) afficher les résultats (ici avec ggplot2)

<span style="color:red"> OK, so the prof was not helpful here on what to do with lsoda. What I did here was search the documentation by typing `?lsoda` in the console and hitting "enter". This will open up a "help" panel with the documentation for the function. Incredibly helpful and beautiful for understanding functions !! </span>

<span style="color:red"> *Note: `?lsoda` only works if the package has been loaded via `library()`! if you want to search all libraries in R, use two question marks: `??lsoda`</span>
```{r}
library(deSolve)
# Execute this in your own Rstudio environment!
?lsoda
```

<span style="color:red"> To note here tho, this documentation is ridiculously intimidating. Since I am allergic to reading, I skipped my merry way right down to the bottom of the page where there's the section "Examples". Example 1 there, "a simple resource limited lotka-volterra-model", is literally exactly what we're trying to do!! So naturally, I copy-pasted that directly into my own RMarkdown. </span>

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# COPIED FROM THE HELP PAGE FOR LSODA !!!

## =======================================================================
## Example 1:
##   A simple resource limited Lotka-Volterra-Model
##
## Note:
## 1. parameter and state variable names made
##    accessible via "with" function
## 2. function sigimp accessible through lexical scoping
##    (see also ode and rk examples)
## =======================================================================

SPCmod <- function(t, x, parms) {
  with(as.list(c(parms, x)), {
    import <- sigimp(t)
    dS <- import - b*S*P + g*C     #substrate
    dP <- c*S*P  - d*C*P           #producer
    dC <- e*P*C  - f*C             #consumer
    res <- c(dS, dP, dC)
    list(res)
  })
}

## Parameters
parms  <- c(b = 0.0, c = 0.1, d = 0.1, e = 0.1, f = 0.1, g = 0.0)

## vector of timesteps
times  <- seq(0, 100, length = 101)

## external signal with rectangle impulse
signal <- as.data.frame(list(times = times,
                            import = rep(0,length(times))))

signal$import[signal$times >= 10 & signal$times <= 11] <- 0.2

sigimp <- approxfun(signal$times, signal$import, rule = 2)


## Start values for steady state
y <- xstart <- c(S = 1, P = 1, C = 1)

## Solving
out <-  lsoda(xstart, times, SPCmod, parms)

## Plotting
mf <- par("mfrow")
plot(out, main = c("substrate", "producer", "consumer"))
plot(out[,"P"], out[,"C"], type = "l", xlab = "producer", ylab = "consumer")
par(mfrow = mf)
```

<span style="color:red"> After copy-pasting, I figured out what to keep, what to scrap, and what to change. Off the bat it's evident that `SCPMod` is important and effectively consists of a list of dX equations. We can do that. There's this weird part `signal` but I don't think that concerns us, so I simply cut it out. There's also `times` and `xstart` variable that seem relevant to adapt for our dataset. </span>

```{r}
# OUR VERSION OF THE ABOVE CODE

## Parameters -- for us r, a, e, and m
parms <- c("r" = 0.5, "a" = 0.1, "e" = 0.9, "m" = 0.5)

## The model function definition. Copy paste of SPCMod, only changed the lines from dP to res to reflect OUR differentials.
PZmod <- function(t, x, parms) {
  with(as.list(c(parms, x)), {
    dP <- r*P - a*P*Z
    dZ <- e*a*P*Z - m*Z
    res <- c(dP, dZ)
    list(res)
  })
}

## Start values, matching the values that we passed to mespop[1,1] and mespop[2,1]
xstart <- c(P = 12, Z = 6)

# Note that i did NOT define times, it was already defined way back in that first snippet that the prof gave us !

# Call to lsoda, changed the name of SCPmod to PZmod but otherwise no modifications
out <- lsoda(xstart, times, PZmod, parms)

head(out)
```
<span style="color:red"> In terms of plotting I possibly overcomplicated a bit compared to just working with base R plots, however I love ggplot2. What's important is being conscientious about the axes, which we specify using `aes()` </span>

<span style="color:red"> I'd like to point out that I use a function `pivot_longer()` here. The reason for this is that in `ggplot2`, if you want to plot lines for each group, it is MUCH easier to have one column "group" with values "group1", "group2", etc. rather than having separate columns "group1", "group2" (a.k.a. the output of `lsoda`). `pivot_longer()` is designed to do that lil transformation for you. </span>

```{r}
library(tidyr) # for pivot_longer

ugly_lotsofcolumns <- data.frame(time = 1:5,
                                 group1 = c(7, 8, 9, 0, 9), 
                                 group2 = c(8, 9, 7, 9, 0),
                                 group3 = c(7, 7, 8, 9, 0),
                                 group4 = c(5, 6, 7, 9, 0))

ugly_lotsofcolumns

pretty_lesscolumns <- ugly_lotsofcolumns |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    group1:group4, # which columns we collapse. Here everything btwn groups 1 and 4
    names_to = "group", # the name of the new "group" column
    values_to = "value", # the name for the column containing the values of group
  )

pretty_lesscolumns |> head()
```
<span style="color:red"> Since we are going to be generating a BUNCH of plots from lsoda output, I'm going to create a function that takes in `lsoda_out` and a `title` and generates the plots we need. </span>

```{r}
library(ggpubr) # for putting two plots side by side. OPTIONAL.

#' Returns side-by-side proie-prédateur simulation and phase portrait for an lsoda result.
#' @param lsoda_out matrix, lsoda output
#' @param title string, the title for the simulation half of the plot
#' @returns plot
lsoda_plot <- function(lsoda_out, title) {
  
  # First we transform the lsoda output from a matrix to a dataframe (otherwise pivot_longer won't work)
  # Then we call pivot_longer
  lsoda_plottable <- lsoda_out |> 
    data.frame() |> 
    pivot_longer(
      P:Z, # we select all columns between P and Z (so P and Z)
      names_to = "species", 
      values_to = "effectif"
    )
  
  # Plot 1: Simulation prey-predator as a function of time
  sim <- ggplot(lsoda_plottable, 
                # aes defines our axes based on the names of columns in lsoda_plottable
                aes(
                  x = time, # x-axis = time
                  y = effectif, # y-axis = effectif
                  col = species) # each species (P or Z) will be plotted w a separate color
                ) +
    geom_line() + # add a line plot
    labs(x = "Temps", y = "Effectif", col = "Species", 
         title = title) +  # Note use of the "title" argument for our function here !
    theme_bw() + # removes ugly grey background
    theme(legend.position = "bottom") # moves the legend to the bottom
  
  # Plot 2: Phase portrait
  # Note that here we're just using lsoda_out directly since we need separate columns for P and Z
  phase <- ggplot(lsoda_out, 
                  aes(
                    x = P, # x-axis = phytoplankton effectif
                    y = Z) # y-axis = zooplankton effectif
                  ) +
    geom_point(cex=0.5) + # make the points smaller
    labs(x = "Effectif de P", y = "Effectif de Z", title = "Portrait de phase") + 
    theme_bw()  # removes ugly grey background
  
  # this is similar to par() in that it will put the plots next to each other
  ggpubr::ggarrange(sim, phase, ncol=2)
}

# Let's see what we get!
lsoda_plot(out, "Simulation proie-prédateur")
```

# Exercise 2: Simuler le modèle de Lotka-Volterra avec une croissance logistique pour la proie

Vous devrez définir de nouveaux paramètres et modifier les équations de votre modèle…

A vous de jouer ici !

<span style="color:red"> Ok, so she's asking us to effectively do the exact same thing we just did in part 1, except this time modify the growth parameter of the phytoplankton to use logistic growth. Logistic growth was covered in class (Modèle de Croissance Verhulst), rather than $rP$ we have $rP(1-\frac{P}{k})$.</span>

<span style="color:red"> In terms of the coding side, we need to modify our PZmod function since our calculation for `dP` is changing. We also have a new parameter, `k`, to add to `parms`. </span>

<span style="color:red"> In terms of getting the plot to look like the profs... trial and error with different values of `k`.</span>

```{r}
# Note new parameter "k"
parms_log <- c("r" = 0.5, "k" = 20, "a" = .1, "e" = .9, "m" = .5)

# New PZ model calculation
PZmod_logistique <- function(t, x, parms) {
  with(as.list(c(parms, x)), {
    # Croissance logistique rP(1-P/k), ou k = capacité limité
    # linear predation does not change
    dP <- r*P*(1 - P/k) - a*Z*P
    dZ <- e*a*P*Z - m*Z
    res <- c(dP, dZ)
    list(res)
  })
}

# xstart and times have not changed so no need to redefine them !
out_log <- lsoda(xstart, times, PZmod_logistique, parms_log)

# Using our plotting function
lsoda_plot(out_log, "Simulation Logistique")
```

# 3. Simuler le modèle de Lotka-Volterra avec une saturation de la prédation

Dans le modèle de Lotka-Volterra de base, toutes les relations sont linéaires. Or ce n’est pas très réalise d’avoir de la prédation linéaire, car plus le prédateur mange plus il est rassasié. A votre avis comment pourrions-nous le représenter ? Par quoi faudrait-il remplacer cette relation linéaire ? Souvenez-vous des réponses fonctionnelles proposées par Holling. Que choisiriez-vous ?

<span style="color:red">So this isn't quite clearly conveyed, for each of these questions 2 onwards we're not building off of the previous question but rather exercise 1, with the purely linear `PZmod` setup !</span>

<span style="color:red">We should probs swap out w a functional response that reflects a decrease when the predator is satistified => Response 2 (Monod/Hyperbolic) from class, $f(R) = \frac{R}{k + R}$. Note that the "resource" here is the Phytoplankton, therefore we're modifying the coefficient on $Z$ rather than $P$. Thus $eaPZ$ becomes $ea(\frac{P}{k + P})Z$. </span>

<span style="color:red">Just like exercise 2, the only things we need to change are `PZmod` and `parms` since we're adding a new parameter `k`. </span>

```{r}
# k chosen by trial and error
parms_satpop <- c("r" = 0.5, "k"=20, "a" = .1, "e" = .9, "m" = .5)

PZmod_satpop <- function(t, x, parms) {
  with(as.list(c(parms, x)), {
    # type 2 response P/(k + P)
    dP <- r*P - e*a*(P/(k + P))*Z
    dZ <- e*a*(P/(k + P))*Z - m*Z
    res <- c(dP, dZ)
    list(res)
  })
}

out_satpop <- lsoda(xstart, times, PZmod_satpop, parms_satpop)

lsoda_plot(out_satpop, "Simulation avec Saturation")
```

# 4. Simuler le modèle de Lotka Volterra avec un mortalité densité dépendante pour le prédateur

Dans le modèle de Lotka-Volterra de base, toutes les relations sont linéaires. Or ce n’est pas très réalise d’avoir de la mortalité linéaire, car plus il y a de prédateurs, plus sa mortalité augmente. On parle de mortalité densité-dépendante. Comment représsenter ça dans le modèle ?

<span style="color:red"> We learned about this one in "Modèles simples et intégration numérique" in the section on "modèles de croissance". So far we've been working with a modèle de Malthus, but a density-dependent model would rather be the modèle de croissance verhulst. We thus replace the linear $mZ$ with the density correction parameter $mZ^2$. </span>

<span style="color:red"> lil note here, the time-effectif plot they show in the TP file doesn't show the zooplankton. I'm p sure they just forgot to add zooplankton to the plot here bc the scale stops at 10. </span>

```{r}
# Parameters actually does not need to change this time, so we don't redefine it !

PZmod_mordens <- function(t, x, parms) {
  with(as.list(c(parms, x)), {
    dP <- r*P - a*P*Z
    # Altered mortality, replacement with m(Z^2)
    dZ <- e*a*P*Z - m*(Z**2) # Z^2 and Z**2 are equivalent
    res <- c(dP, dZ)
    list(res)
  })
}

out_mordens <- lsoda(xstart, times, PZmod_mordens, parms)

lsoda_plot(out_mordens, "Mortalité Densité")
```

Et si m vaut 0.3, qu’obtenez-vous ? Quel est le type d’équilibre ?

parms_mordens_m3 <- c("r" = 0.5, "a" = .1, "e" = .9, "m" = .3)

# 5. Simuler le modèle de Lotka-Volterra avec 3 niveaux trophiques 

Nous allons maintenant un peu changer les valeurs des paramètres et voir le comportement du modèle change.

<span style="color:red"> Ok so we see this figure of a model with three tiers -- phytoplankton, zooplankton, fish. We thus need to imagine a new set of differential equations to reflect the newcomer. Let's say that the fish eats zooplankton. </span>

<span style="color:red"> If we extend the model that we used to create the Z/P equations, we can consider that rather than zooplankton mortality being $mZ$, it's rather mortality by predation from fish, $a_fZF$. The equation for fish is then $\frac{dF}{dt} = cF - mF = e_fa_fZF - mF$.</span>

<span style="color:red"> In order to add this to our code, we have to add an extra line specifying the equation for $dFi$ (note that `F` can't be used because it correlates to `FALSE`) and make sure it becomes part of our result. Note that the parameters `a` and `e` are now specialized for either fish (`af` and `ef`) or zooplankton (`az` and `ez`)</span>

```{r}
parms_pzf <- c("r" = .7, "az" = 0.35, "af" = 0.3, "ez" = 0.5, "ef" = 0.8, "m" = 0.4)

PZFimod <- function(t, x, parms) {
  with(as.list(c(parms, x)), {
    dP <- r*P - az*P*Z
    dZ <- ez*az*P*Z - af*Z*Fi # replacement of m*Z with af*Z*Fi
    dFi <- ef*af*Z*Fi - m*Fi # new line defining dFi
    res <- c(dP, dZ, dFi) # addition of Fi
    list(res)
  })
}

# We also need to define a new xstart now that we have a third parameter.
# I chose 3 because it's half of 6
xstart_pzf <- c(P = 12, Z = 6, Fi = 3)

out_pzf <- lsoda(xstart_pzf, times, PZFimod, parms_pzf)

head(out_pzf)
```
Now in terms of generating plots, we can't use our handy dandy `lsoda_plot()` because it wouldn't know what to do with Fish. However, because we want to do something nearly identical, we're gonna pull the classic copy -> paste -> edit what needs to change.

```{r}

#' Returns proie-prédateur simulation and phase portraits for an lsoda result for P, Z, and Fi.
#' @param lsoda_out matrix, lsoda output
#' @param title string, the title for the simulation plot
#' @returns list of plots
lsoda_plot_pzf <- function(lsoda_out, title) {
  
  lsoda_plottable <- lsoda_out |> 
    data.frame() |> 
    pivot_longer(
      P:Fi, # change to select from P to Fi rather than P to Z
      names_to = "species", 
      values_to = "effectif"
    )
  
  # Plot 1: Simulation prey-predator as a function of time
  # No change !
  simulation <- ggplot(lsoda_plottable, 
                aes(
                  x = time, 
                  y = effectif, 
                  col = species) 
                ) +
    geom_line() + 
    labs(x = "Temps", y = "Effectif", col = "Species", 
         title = title) +  
    theme_bw() + 
    theme(legend.position = "bottom") 
  
  # Plot 2: Phase portrait of Phytoplankton vs. Zooplankton
  # Also no change !
  phasePZ <- ggplot(lsoda_out, 
                  aes(
                    x = P, 
                    y = Z) 
                  ) +
    geom_point(cex=0.5) + 
    labs(x = "Effectif de P", y = "Effectif de Z", title = "Portrait de phase") + 
    theme_bw()
  
  # Plot 3: Phase portrait of Zooplankton vs. Fish (New)
  # basically the same as plot 2, we just change the axes a bit
  phaseZFi <- ggplot(lsoda_out, 
                  aes(
                    x = Z, 
                    y = Fi) 
                  ) +
    geom_point(cex=0.5) + 
    labs(x = "Effectif de Z", y = "Effectif de Fi", title = "Portrait de phase") + 
    theme_bw()
  
  # With 3 plots, arranging them side by side would be hard to read
  # I'm instead just going to return a list of all the plots
  # giving them names is entirely optional
  c("Simulation" = simulation, "PhasePZ" = phasePZ, "PhaseZFi" = phaseZFi)
}

# test it out
lsoda_plot_pzf(out_pzf, "Simulation PZF")
```

## Et que se passe-t-il pour une mortalité quadratique des poissons ?

<span style="color:red"> Quadratic mortality corresponds to density-dependent mortality (modèle de croissance verhulst. All we need to do is swap out `m*Fi` for `m*Fi^2`. </span>

```{r}
PZFimod_quad <- function(t, x, parms) {
  with(as.list(c(parms, x)), {
    dP <- r*P - az*P*Z
    dZ <- ez*az*P*Z - af*Z*Fi
    dFi <- ef*af*Z*Fi - m*Fi^2 # quadratic mortality
    res <- c(dP, dZ, dFi)
    list(res)
  })
}

out_pzf_quad <- lsoda(xstart_pzf, times, PZFimod_quad, parms_pzf)

plot_res <- lsoda_plot_pzf(out_pzf_quad, "Simulation PZF - Mortalité quadratique")
plot_res
```
